extracted.intended_audience: general readers; literary and religious-criticism audience interested in Mark Twain's critique of Christian Science
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-critical essay (book-chapter excerpt) that evaluates the doctrines, organization, finances, growth prospects, and writings of Mary Baker Eddy and the Christian Science movement. It mixes social prediction, moral judgment, and stylistic critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization and monopoly (Annex, capitation tax)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mother-Church Headquarters Factory in Boston monopolizes Christian-Science literary discharges; acquisition and practice require purchase of official materials and payment of fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original examples: 'One hundred dollars for it.' 'No member, young or old, of a branch Christian-Scientist church can acquire and retain membership in the Mother-Church unless he pay “capitation tax” (of “not less than a dollar,” say the By-Laws) to the Boston Trust every year.' Scoring/implication: measure a religion/organization by how much it monetizes access to doctrine and membership; anti-pattern is compulsory purchases and recurring mandatory dues that function as reliable income streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory possession of official texts as a gatekeeping requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: No healer, Metaphysical-College-bred or other, is allowed to practice unless he possesses a copy of Mrs. Eddy's Annex (the 'Bible-Annex').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'In order to force the sale of Mrs Eddy's Bible-Annex, no healer... is allowed to practice the game unless he possesses a copy of that book.' Use this as a criterion for institutional gatekeeping and monetized credentialing; an anti-pattern is forcing practitioners to buy proprietary texts to practice the faith/healing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of potential income and centralized financial power
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralized sales (Annex, capitation taxes, pilgrimages, merchandise) are projected to yield immense annual income, giving the Trust enormous financial strength and political leverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's projection examples: estimates of 'millions' and later 'an income approaching five million dollars a day.' Use as an evaluative metric: estimate revenue streams and concentration of cash to judge likely social/political power. Warning: large centralized funds with no external accountability concentrate power and increase risk of abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial opacity and evasive testimony about expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trust does not disclose how it spends money; inquiries elicit evasive answers such as 'we must have faith in Our Mother' or that matters have been 'demonstrated over.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted behavior: 'To this day, after all our diligence, we have not been able to get it to confess what it does with the money.' Use transparency as a criterion: lack of accounting or evasive ritual-language responses indicate opacity and justify suspicion. Anti-pattern: answering financial questions with spiritual platitudes rather than accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of visible charitable expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: No discoverable evidence that the Trust spends funds on typical charities (orphans, hospitals, missions, libraries, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's observation: 'I have hunted, hunted, and hunted... and have not yet got upon the track of a farthing that the Trust has spent upon any worthy object.' Use philanthropic giving (or lack thereof) as an indicator of organizational priorities; scoring: organizations that hoard funds or do not publicize charitable activity score poorly on social-responsibility measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization of ritual and shrine (paid pilgrimages and merchandise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious rites and pilgrimages are monetized: 'the annual Pilgrimage to Mrs. Eddy's tomb, from all over the world—admission, the Christian-Science Dollar (payable in advance)—purchases of consecrated glass beads, candles, memorial spoons, aureoled chrome-portraits and bogus autographs of Mrs. Eddy... cash for miracles worked at the tomb.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the extent to which rites, sacraments, or pilgrimages are turned into paid commodities as a rubric for commodification; examples here enumerate specific merchandise and paid events as revenue sources. Anti-pattern: ritual-as-revenue rather than spiritual service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of authority leading to potential political dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact, centralized Trust controlling doctrine and funds can translate into political influence and future governing power ('in America in 1920 the Christian Scientists will be a political force... in 1940 the governing power in the Republic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate movements by organizational centralization and fundraising scale as predictors of political capability. The author warns that centralization + cash + communication control (railway, telegraph, subsidized newspapers) yield unprecedented ability to watch and manage an empire—score high for potential political threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and institutionalization of a common human faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement's core success lies in taking a universal human capacity (imagination/placebo-like healing) and organizing it, backing it with capital, and concentrating it at headquarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'The Christian Scientist has taken a force which has been lying idle in every member of the human race since time began, and has organized it, and backed the business with capital...' Use institutionalization of common practices as a criterion: formalizing and monetizing a ubiquitous human behavior can make a movement powerful and widely adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment as primary driver of conversion and spread
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversions are overwhelmingly driven by environment, family, and association rather than by intellectual argument: 'Environment is the chief thing to be considered when one is proposing to predict the future of Christian Science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the social-environmental embeddedness (family units, local clusters) as a metric for likely growth; examples: families acting as 'factories' of recruits. Anti-pattern: assuming intellectual appeal correlates with spread—author argues the opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and social appeal over intellectual argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian Science 'makes no embarrassing appeal to the intellect' and succeeds because it appeals to feelings and environment rather than reasoned inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess movements by whether they primarily engage emotion/feeling versus reasoned, evidence-based argument. Scoring: high emotional/association appeal predicts broad uptake among 'ninety-nine one-hundredths of the human race' per author; intellectual rigor is not required for mass appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of lay adherents as an independent evaluative fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay members are said to be 'entirely sincere in their faith,' and sincerity merits respect irrespective of the trust's institutional practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: distinguish institutional critique from respect for individual believers' sincerity. Measure: sincerity and zeal of adherents are real and can be socially powerful even if leadership acts questionably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of healing framed as mutual imagination (patient + healer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Healing requires two imaginations—the patient's and an outsider's—so the outsider (healer) functions like an engineer who 'turns on the steam'; the healer's services are necessary and chargeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this psychological/placebo interpretation as a criterion to evaluate claims of healing: whether cures appear attributable to social/psychological intervention rather than metaphysical laws. Policy implication: recognize practical value of healer's role even if metaphysical claims are doubted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evasive, foggy, or garrulous testimony as a characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian-Science testimony is 'generally foggy, generally diffuse, generally garrulous,' often adding meaningless words to otherwise direct statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess communications for clarity and precision; fogginess and ritualized evasions (e.g., 'demonstrated over') indicate rhetorical, not evidentiary, modes of discourse. Anti-pattern: treating spiritual-sounding evasions as substantive answers to concrete questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary quality and consistency of doctrinal writings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Eddy's Bible and Science and Health underwent revisions that improved English style—'The English is clean, compact, dignified, almost perfect'—but her prose sometimes collapses back into awkwardness and obscurity, especially when applied beyond its core subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a leader's written works for clarity, grammatical competence, and consistency across subjects; measure revisions' effects and look for failure modes (good prose on core topics; bad or obscure prose when range broadens). Example antipattern: dignified phrasing in later revisions contrasted with awkward earlier passages and occasional regressions.
